title: The water cycle in a glass valley

bodies.name: Ridge
bodies.label: Ridge
bodies.describe: Wind forces the moist air up its slope; rising air expands and cools.

bodies.name: Lake
bodies.label: Lake · source of vapour
bodies.describe: Sunshine warms the water and the air above it; molecules escape as vapour.

bodies.name: Water vapour
bodies.label: Water vapour
bodies.describe: An invisible gas in reality; drawn here as faint motes rising from the lake.

bodies.name: Air parcel
bodies.label: Air parcel · moist air from the lake
bodies.describe: One rising bubble of lake air: you can ride it (POV).

bodies.name: Cloud
bodies.label: Cloud · condensed droplets
bodies.describe: Droplets condensed from the vapour; it greys as it fills with water.

bodies.name: Windsock
bodies.label: Wind · carries the cloud to the ridge
bodies.describe: It blows from the lake towards the ridge; the sock lifts as the wind strengthens.

bodies.name: Rain
bodies.label: Rain
bodies.describe: Falls once the cloud holds more water than its droplets can keep aloft.

bodies.name: Sun
bodies.label: Sun · the energy source
bodies.describe: Its height through the day sets how strongly the lake is heated; the light and the shadows come from it.

dew point.label: rising air cools 9.8 K per km

windward slope.label: forced up the slope, it cools

rain shadow.label: sinking air warms; the cloud evaporates

lessons.title: Heat the lake
lessons.question: What lifts water out of the lake?
lessons.text: Turn the sunshine up. Watch how the vapour rises faster from the lake, and watch three readouts: the lake-air temperature, the saturation vapour pressure e_s, and the evaporation rate.
lessons.explain: Stronger sunshine warms the lake air from 22.2 to 28.7 °C. The saturation vapour pressure e_s rises from 26.6 to 39.2 hPa, about 6 % per kelvin: the Clausius–Clapeyron rate (Koutsoyiannis 2012). Evaporation is driven by the gap between e_s and the vapour already in the air, so it more than doubles, from 1.4 to 3.4 mm a day. Saturation is a property of water at a given temperature. It is not a capacity of the air.

lessons.title: Ride a parcel of air
lessons.question: Where does the vapour go?
lessons.text: You are now inside one parcel of moist lake air as it rises. Look up: the cloud base is above you. Wait until the parcel reaches its dew point.
lessons.explain: Rising air expands and cools by 9.8 K per kilometre while it is unsaturated. Its dew point falls only about 1.8 K per kilometre, so the gap between them closes by about 8 K per kilometre. The parcel therefore saturates about 125 m higher for every kelvin of gap at the ground (Espy). Here the lake air is at 28.9 °C with a dew point of 25.4 °C, a gap of 3.5 K, so condensation starts near 436 m, at 24.7 °C. There the vapour condenses on tiny aerosol particles into cloud droplets.
lessons.opens: Why does the rain fall on the ridge and not on the lake?

lessons.title: Wind to the ridge
lessons.question: Why does the rain fall on the ridge and not on the lake?
lessons.text: Raise the wind. The cloud drifts from the lake to the ridge and climbs its windward slope. Watch the cloud water readouts and wait for rain.
lessons.explain: Over the lake the cloud held only about 0.2–0.3 g of droplets per kg of air, too little to rain. Forced 329 m up the slope, it cooled from about 24.1 to 22.7 °C, along the moist adiabat: about 4 K per km in warm, wet air, because condensing vapour releases latent heat. Each kelvin of cooling lowers e_s by about 6 %, so more vapour condenses. Once the droplets pass 1 g per kg, this model lets them grow into falling drops: orographic rain (Roe 2005).
lessons.opens: What happens to the air beyond the crest?

lessons.title: Over the crest
lessons.question: What happens to the air beyond the crest?
lessons.text: Follow the cloud over the crest of the ridge and down its far side, then wait for the rain shadow.
lessons.explain: Sinking air is compressed and warms. Once its droplets have evaporated it warms at the dry rate of 9.8 K per km, faster than it cooled on the way up while it was condensing. It also left water on the windward slope as rain. Brought back to valley level it is 30.6 °C, 1.7 K warmer than when it set out: each gram of water rained out per kg of air leaves 2.5 K of latent heat behind. The far valley gets dry, warm air: a rain shadow, and in strong cases a föhn wind.
lessons.opens: Can a cloud rain without a ridge?

lessons.title: Calm air
lessons.question: Can a cloud rain without a ridge?
lessons.text: Drop the wind almost to zero. The next cloud stays over the warm lake, keeps being fed by rising vapour, and grows deeper. Watch the cloud water over the lake and wait until rain falls back on the lake.
lessons.explain: Without wind, convection keeps feeding the same cloud, and it deepens to almost 1 km. Its upper part climbs further along the moist adiabat and holds more condensed water. Past 1 g per kg it rains back onto the lake, so the cycle closes locally. Across the planet the cycle does not close locally: each year about 40 000 km³ of water evaporated from the oceans is carried by the wind to fall on land, and rivers return it to the sea (Trenberth et al. 2007).
lessons.opens: What sets the pace of the whole cycle?

lessons.title: Evening
lessons.question: What sets the pace of the whole cycle?
lessons.text: Move the time of day to evening. With the sun low, watch the lake-air temperature, e_s and the evaporation rate fall.
lessons.explain: At 18:30 the sun gives almost no heat. The lake air cools to 10.2 °C, and e_s falls to 12.5 hPa, less than a third of its midday value. The air above the lake is now saturated, so evaporation stops and mist forms over the water. The sun powers the cycle: evaporating one kilogram of water takes about 2.45 MJ, and gravity brings the water back down.
